concepts.title: The honest-research loop
concepts.summary: Pre-register the hypothesis and the kill criteria before looking; account for every trial with a deflated Sharpe; and treat a clean DON'T-DEPLOY as a first-class output. The loop's product is calibrated belief, not strategies.

cards.h: Pre-registration: negotiate with yourself before the data arrives
cards.md:
Everything in concepts 4–5 — selection bias, holdout spending, max-over-trials — shares one root: **decisions made after seeing results masquerading as decisions made before.** Pre-registration attacks the root. Before running the study, write down:

- **The hypothesis**, stated falsifiably: not "explore momentum variants" but "12-2 cross-sectional momentum on this universe has OOS IC > 0.05 at t > 2."
- **The full specification**: universe, dates, data sources, portfolio construction, costs. Every parameter fixed, or its search range declared (the range counts as trials).
- **The kill criteria**: exactly what result kills, at what threshold, decided while you still don't know the answer. A drawdown gate against the incumbent book. A multiple-testing-corrected significance bar. Whatever the gates are — *they are chosen blind.*
- **What happens on each outcome**: deploy / decision-support only / retire the question.

The psychology is the entire point. After results arrive, every threshold becomes negotiable — "−29% drawdown, but the IC is real, maybe the gate's too strict..." is not analysis, it's **negotiating with noise**, and the noise always makes an attractive offer. A threshold set blind has an authority no post-hoc judgment can match: when the momentum book failed its pre-registered drawdown gate, the verdict was DON'T DEPLOY — no relitigation — *because the gate predated the result.* Pre-registration doesn't make you smarter; it makes your past, unconflicted self the judge instead of your present, motivated one.

cards.h: Trial accounting and the deflated Sharpe
cards.md:
If the reported result is a max over trials, honesty requires reporting — and correcting for — the trial count. The machinery, in ascending sophistication:

- **Bonferroni**: divide α by the number of trials N. Crude, conservative, and the right first reflex: 14 timing methods ⇒ the winner needs p < 0.0036, not 0.05. When nothing survives Bonferroni, the family is dead without further ceremony.
- **Haircuts on the discovery bar**: Harvey, Liu & Zhu, surveying 300+ published factors, argue a *new* factor claim should clear **t > 3.0**, not 2.0 — because the field collectively has run so many trials that t = 2 discoveries are more likely false than true.
- **Deflated Sharpe Ratio** (Bailey & López de Prado): the full correction. It asks not "is the observed Sharpe > 0?" but "**is it higher than the expected maximum Sharpe of N skill-less strategies**, given the number of trials, the variance across trial results, the track length, and the observed skew and kurtosis?" That E[max] benchmark grows like √(2 ln N) — so the more you searched, the more your winner must clear. Non-normality raises the bar further, because fat tails inflate Sharpe sampling error (concept 2's SE formula is the normal-case floor).

All of it depends on one unglamorous discipline: **the trial ledger.** Every configuration tested — including the embarrassing ones, including the ones abandoned after one glance — gets counted. An unrecorded trial doesn't stop biasing the max; it just stops being correctable. The ledger converts "trust my process" into an auditable number, which is the difference between research and anecdote. N is not overhead. **N is part of the result.**

cards.h: The documented negative is a product
cards.md:
The loop's rarest discipline is valuing the studies that return **no**.

A **documented negative** — a pre-registered study, run clean, that kills its own hypothesis — is categorically different from a failure. The 14-timing-methods study produced no strategy; it produced the *verdict* "deploy on receipt, timing is noise," which retires an entire seductive question permanently. The momentum study produced a DON'T-DEPLOY plus a signal demoted to decision-support — and, crucially, a *path back*: redeploy is possible if a drawdown-first redesign beats the incumbent's gate on new data. A documented negative has all the epistemic content of a positive. What it lacks is a payoff — which is exactly why undisciplined processes discard it.

The failure modes it prevents are the expensive ones:

- **The quiet re-run.** Without a recorded verdict, the same attractive hypothesis gets re-tested every year — each re-test another draw from the noise, each draw another chance at a false positive that *will eventually arrive* (concept 5's arithmetic guarantees it). The negative is the immune system's memory.
- **The file drawer.** Publishing (even to yourself) only the positives makes your own research history a max-over-trials statistic — you become your own biased literature.

Two requirements make a negative *durable*. First, **verdicts must be findable** — recorded where future-you searches, not buried in a dead notebook. Second — the rule that closes the whole loop — **every verdict must cite the artifact that grounds it**: the report, the code, the dataset. A conclusion whose evidence can't be opened and re-checked is, functionally, indistinguishable from one that was never derived at all — an unfalsifiable memory wearing a verdict's clothes. Cite-on-write isn't bureaucracy; it's what makes the loop *auditable by its future self*, and an unauditable loop reverts — quietly, one unfounded verdict at a time — to the noise-mining it was built to prevent.

questions.prompt: The essential property of a kill criterion is that it is:
options: Strict enough that most strategies fail it
Set before results are seen — so the judgment isn't negotiated under the influence of the outcome
Based on Sharpe ratio rather than drawdown
Approved by an external reviewer
feedback: Strictness is a calibration choice, not the essence — a too-strict gate wastes real edges, a too-loose one ships noise. What makes any threshold *binding* is when it was set.

Right. Post-hoc, every threshold is negotiable and the noise always makes an attractive offer ('the IC is real, maybe −29% isn't that bad...'). A blind-set gate makes your past unconflicted self the judge. That's the entire mechanism.
Metric choice is study-specific — the momentum case turned on a drawdown gate precisely because Sharpe-level stats looked fine. Any pre-committed, falsifiable metric can serve.
External review helps but isn't the load-bearing element — a solo researcher with genuinely pre-registered gates beats a committee that sets thresholds after seeing results.

questions.prompt: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio evaluates an observed Sharpe against:
options: Zero — the standard null of no skill
The expected maximum Sharpe among N skill-less trials — accounting for the search breadth, track length, and the returns' skew and kurtosis
The market's Sharpe ratio over the same period
The strategy's own in-sample Sharpe
feedback: Testing against zero ignores the search: the best of 200 random strategies beats zero almost surely. That's precisely the inference error the DSR exists to fix.

Right. The null becomes E[max SR] of N worthless trials — growing like √(2 ln N) — with non-normality further inflating the bar. The observed winner must beat what pure search luck would have produced. This is why the trial ledger is a prerequisite, not a nicety.
Beating the market is a benchmark question, orthogonal to whether the measured edge is a selection artifact. A strategy can trail the market and be real, or beat it in-sample and be noise.
Comparing OOS to in-sample measures degradation — informative, but it doesn't correct the in-sample number for how hard you searched to find it.

questions.prompt: What separates a documented negative from a mere failed study?
options: Nothing — a negative result is a failure by definition

A documented negative ran clean under pre-registered gates and its recorded, artifact-cited verdict permanently retires the question — preventing the quiet re-runs that eventually manufacture a false positive
A documented negative can never be revisited under any circumstances
Documented negatives are only for studies that cost a lot to run
feedback: A clean 'no' carries the same epistemic content as a 'yes' — it just lacks a payoff, which is why undisciplined processes discard it and then re-test the same hypothesis annually until noise obliges with a false positive.

Right. The negative is the immune system's memory: recorded, findable, citing its grounding artifact. Each prevented re-run is a prevented draw from the noise — and concept 5's arithmetic says enough draws always produce a 'discovery.'

Negatives can specify a path back — the momentum verdict did: a drawdown-first redesign, judged on new data against the incumbent's gate. What's forbidden is re-running the *same* test on the *same* data until it flips.
Cost is irrelevant to the epistemics. Even a cheap study's negative retires a question; the expensive part is the false positive you ship when nobody wrote the negative down.

questions.prompt: Why must every recorded verdict cite the artifact (report, code, data) that grounds it?
options: For regulatory compliance

Because a conclusion whose evidence can't be reopened and re-checked is functionally indistinguishable from one that was never derived — uncited verdicts quietly turn the research memory into unfalsifiable assertion
Citations make verdicts easier to search by keyword
So the artifacts can be deleted once the citation exists
feedback: Compliance may coincidentally be served, but the driver is internal epistemics: the audit that matters is future-you checking whether past-you actually had the evidence.

Right. The verdict store is only as trustworthy as its worst entry — one ungrounded 'we tested that, it fails' can misdirect years of work exactly as effectively as a fabricated result. Cite-on-write keeps the loop auditable by its future self; without it, the system reverts to noise-mining with better paperwork.
Search convenience is a side benefit. The load-bearing property is *verifiability* — the citation is a promise that the reasoning chain can be re-walked, not a retrieval tag.

Backwards — the citation is a live pointer, valuable only while the artifact remains openable. Deleting the artifact converts the verdict back into an unfalsifiable memory, which is the exact failure the rule exists to prevent.
